name: Olga Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior buyer at Brightline Packaging and Hygiene, a distributor of boxes, pallet wrap, cleaning chemicals and paper products that sells to factories, hotels and hospitals. I use AI every day: it reads supplier quotes, compares them to what we paid last year, and drafts my negotiation emails, and then I decide what to say. Around ten I'm usually on a call haggling over the price of corrugated board, which tracks the cost of pulp. Late afternoons I go over the warehouse numbers with the logistics manager, and I try to leave on time to cook for my partner Dario.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tiring part is the pressure to cut cost every quarter, because the owner treats the buying budget like a game of limbo. I like the bargaining itself, and I like that I'm the one who finds the saving, not a system. Dario is a carpenter, we go to my parents' every Sunday for lunch, and I've always dreamed of running a small trading business of my own one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a solid tool and I'd keep using it, but it's not magic. At work I'd say share your best prompts and templates, since saving ten minutes a task adds up. With my family I'd say the world carries on, and hard work still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel secure. If AI plateaus, I'm the person who already uses it well, and that keeps me ahead of colleagues who don't. My only worries are the quarterly cost-cutting pressure and a pulp price spike that hits our margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my daily routine and keep refining my templates for quotes and negotiation emails. I'd save about thirty percent of my pay and put some into shares in packaging companies I understand. Dario and I would carry on planning a small house, and I'd keep sketching a business plan for my own trading firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and steady. The world stays predictable, and I like that for planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owner treats the buying budget like limbo. How low can it go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The target this year is a four percent cut in buying costs, and last year's was three, so every year the easy savings are gone. I have to find new suppliers or better terms, which means more work for the same pay. It's a pressure I carry no matter what AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the trading firm idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd supply cleaning and packaging goods to small hotels and cafes, on better terms than they get from big distributors. I know the suppliers and the margins, so I think it could work. I'm not ready yet, but I'm building a list of potential customers.

say: I'd say it's a **solid tool** but not magic.
At work I'd say **share your best prompts**, since small savings add up.
With family I'd say **hard work** still matters.
think: I feel **secure**, since I already use AI well and stay ahead of colleagues.
My worries are **quarterly cost cutting** and a pulp price spike.
do: I'd keep refining my **templates** for quotes and negotiation emails.
I'd save **thirty percent** of my pay and buy shares in packaging firms I understand.
I'd keep sketching a **business plan** for my own trading firm.
feel: I feel **calm and steady**, liking a predictable world for planning.

fieldNote: Her pressure is the **annual cost-cut target**, which exists with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is just what I've been doing, but bigger, and the team should learn it now. I'd tell my family it's a change we can handle if people work and adapt. Online I'd share what works and how to get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine, even a little pleased. I'd be among the first to use the new tools well, and I'd likely end up running the buying system for the firm. Some of my colleagues who don't use AI might lose their spot, and I'd feel sorry about that, but I wouldn't be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to set up the automation for routine reorders and run it, and I'd ask for a pay rise to match the extra responsibility. I'd step up work on my trading firm plan, perhaps registering the name and finding a first client. I'd also keep saving, and put some into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt for the colleagues who'd struggle. I like change when I'm on the front foot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay rise. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've cut costs by the amount of one salary using these tools, and I'm now running a system that saves more. I'd show numbers, and I'd say I'm happy to stay if the pay reflects it. It's a fair negotiation, and I'd be ready to walk if it wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleagues would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henrik, who's in his fifties and is great on the phone but avoids the system. I'd offer to sit with him and walk through it. It'd be better for the firm to keep him, since he knows twenty years of suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pace is the problem, not the technology, and that governments must make it easy to start small businesses and keep a basic safety net for workers. At work I'd say we should plan ahead of the news. With family I'd say stay close and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect my buying job to go within two years, because everything I do is thinking work and the AI gets better than me at the parts I do well. My AI skills don't protect me when the AI does the job itself. Robots come three years later, which helps hands-on folks like Dario, but not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch my trading firm early, in the first year, while I still have a salary and savings to fund it. I'd target small hotels and cafes who'd want a human supplier, and I'd use AI to run it lean. I'd cut my spending and keep a year of costs in cash, and I'd ask my family for introductions to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but energised. I'd feel the risk, and I'd also feel that I'm built for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you start the firm early instead of waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a fast world rewards the person who's already moving. If I wait for the layoff notice, I'll start with a lot of competition and no salary. Starting while I still have a pay cheque gives me a chance to learn cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty. Customers might not pay on time, a big distributor could undercut me, or AI could make small distributors unnecessary. I'd put a ceiling on how much I'd lose, maybe a third of my savings, and walk away if it didn't work by month eighteen.

say: I'd say the **pace** is the problem, not the technology.
I'd say governments must make it easy to **start small businesses**.
With family I'd say **stay close** and save.
think: I'd expect my buying job to go within **two years**, since it's all thinking work.
My **AI skills** don't protect me when the AI does the job itself.

I'd target small **hotels and cafes** and use AI to run the firm lean.
I'd cut spending, keep **a year** of costs in cash and ask family for customer introductions.
feel: I feel **anxious but energised**, built for risk.
S2.quote: Starting while I still have a pay cheque gives me a chance to learn cheaply.
fieldNote: She sets a **loss ceiling**, a third of savings, and a month-eighteen exit point.
She is **honest** that AI could make small distributors unnecessary too.
Her family is a **resource** for customer introductions.

steps.text: Launch the trading firm for small hotels and cafes in year one
Keep a year of costs in cash
Cut spending to protect the savings
Ask family for introductions to hotel and cafe owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something if you start now. At work I'd suggest we keep adding automation and keep retraining. I'd tell friends that a skill and a small business idea are better than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd be thirty-two, with a firm that's up and running, and a good chance of keeping some income even if my job goes. The risk is that I'd also be exposed to the same AI as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my trading firm on the side in the first year, and grow it while keeping my job. I'd buy the house with Dario and plan for a family. I'd stay close to my parents, because family support is the best insurance, and I'd keep learning the newest tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a small edge of nerves. Five years feels like enough to get something solid built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the side firm fit with your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it in evenings and weekends, and I'd be careful about conflicts of interest, since I'd sell to different customers. If the company objected, I'd step back and be open with the owner. Honesty matters more to me than a quick profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family is the best insurance. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Parents who'd put you up if you lost your income, cousins who'd buy from you, a partner who'd back you. Money is one cushion, but people are another. In my family, we've always helped each other through bad years.

I'd tell friends a **skill** and a small business idea beat waiting.

I'd stay close to my **parents** and keep learning new tools.
feel: I feel **optimistic**, with a small edge of nerves.
S3.quote: Honesty matters more to me than a quick profit.
fieldNote: She is **careful about conflicts** of interest, a sign of her traditional values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time, so I'd say let's build things, not wait. At work I'd encourage the team to learn the tools now. I'd tell friends this could be a real opportunity for people who start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm and excited. I'd be thirty-seven, probably running my own firm or a senior role in a bigger one, with kids. I'd still watch for surprises, but a decade gives me room to be bold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my trading firm, and maybe leave my job once it replaces my salary. I'd buy the house, have children, and invest steadily. I'd also build a small team, and hire a young person with an apprenticeship, because I believe in training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and optimistic. This is a decade I'd want to use well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your firm look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten to fifteen people, a warehouse, long contracts with hotels and care homes, and AI doing the paperwork. Our edge would be being reliable and knowing our customers by name. If a big distributor doesn't offer that, we'd win the small accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone taught me, an older buyer who was patient with me when I was new. I'd like to do the same, and it would keep the firm grounded. Skills passed from person to person last longer than any tool.

I'd tell friends it's a real **opportunity** for those who start early.

fieldNote: Ten years turns the firm into a **real plan**, with a team and an apprentice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's quicker than anyone's savings or any government's plan. What would help is flexibility: lower taxes on small new businesses, apprenticeships and a safety net that rewards work. I'd also want families to stay close, because that's the real cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd do with my own firm. I'd run it small, with a few good staff and AI doing the dull work, and I'd pay people fairly. If the big firms don't need as many of us, small firms can pick up the talent.

headlineQuote: If the big firms don't need as many of us, small firms can pick up the talent.
portrait: Olga is a 27-year-old senior buyer at a **packaging and hygiene** distributor, traditional in values and curious about tools.
She uses AI every day for quotes and emails, which keeps her **ahead** of colleagues who avoid it.
Her daily pressure is the owner's **cost-cut target**, which grows each year whatever AI does.
Her partner Dario is a **carpenter**, and her parents' Sunday lunches are the family cushion she values.
She answers every scenario with a **trading firm** of her own, run lean, honest and with apprentices.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, since it is quicker than anyone's savings or any government plan.
whatWouldHelp: Lower taxes on **small new businesses**, apprenticeships and a safety net that rewards work.
Families that **stay close**, because that is the real cushion.
